# Chapter Plot — ch<NN>

The structured plot for a single chapter. The first agent in the per-chapter pipeline produces this; the scene card agent expands it; the brief agent narrows it; the prose agent writes from the brief.

This file is the macro layer. It answers: "What is this chapter about, and what must it accomplish?"

---

## Identity

- **Chapter number**: <NN>
- **Working title**: <title>
- **Arc**: <which arc this chapter belongs to (e.g. "Arc 2, chapter 5 of 20")>
- **POV**: <character>

---

## Role in the Arc

One paragraph: what does this chapter exist to do at the arc level?

- Is it a setup chapter (planting seeds)?
- A payoff chapter (resolving prior setups)?
- A pivot chapter (changing the direction of the arc)?
- A breather chapter (character beat / world detail)?
- A climactic chapter (arc-level resolution)?

If the chapter doesn't have a clear role, the chapter shouldn't exist yet — go back to the arc design.

---

## Key Scenes (3–6 typical)

Bullet list of the scenes this chapter must include, in order. Each scene gets one line at this stage; the scene card agent will expand each one.

1. <scene one — one-line summary>
2. <scene two — one-line summary>
3. <scene three — one-line summary>
4. ...

---

## Hook (chapter ending)

The last beat of the chapter. What makes the reader want to read the next one?

- **Hook type**: <cliffhanger / revelation / atmospheric / character-moment / question-raised>
- **Specific hook**: <one sentence>

The hook should match the arc-level pacing target. Not every chapter needs a cliffhanger; not every chapter can afford a quiet ending.

---

## Required Story Beats (must land in this chapter)

Things that MUST happen, regardless of how the prose develops:

- <beat — e.g. "Character X learns Character Y is alive">
- <beat — e.g. "The reader sees the antagonist make decision Z">
- <beat>

These are non-negotiable. The plot review lens checks for them.

---

## Forbidden Items (must NOT appear in this chapter)

Things that must NOT show up:

- <forbidden — e.g. "No mention of [future plot element] yet">
- <forbidden — e.g. "Character X's true name must not be spoken aloud">
- <forbidden — e.g. "The reader must not learn fact Y until chapter NN+3">

These are the per-scene/per-chapter forbidden items, distinct from the global `forbidden_patterns.md` (which is about prose style, not story disclosure).

---

## Foreshadowing — plant / payoff

If this chapter plants a seed for later payoff, or pays off a seed planted earlier, document it:

- **Planting**: <seed planted in this chapter, target payoff chapter>
- **Paying off**: <seed planted in ch<NN>, paid off here>

Update `../90_canon/timeline.md` foreshadowing ledger to match.

---

## Connections

- **Previous chapter (ch<NN-1>) ended with**: <one sentence>
- **This chapter starts at**: <time gap from previous? location change?>
- **Next chapter (ch<NN+1>) will need to receive from this one**: <what must be true at chapter end>

---

## Target Length

<word count or character count target>

---

## Notes for the Scene Card Agent

Anything the next stage of the pipeline needs to know that doesn't fit above:

- <note>
- <note>

---

## How Agents Use This File

- **Scene card agent** reads this and expands each "key scene" into a structured scene card.
- **Brief agent** reads this for the macro view, then narrows it to per-scene instructions.
- **Plot review lens** checks the drafted chapter against the "Required Story Beats" and "Forbidden Items" sections.

# Scene Cards — ch<NN>

Per-scene breakdown. The scene card agent expands each "key scene" from the plot file into a structured card. The brief agent then uses these cards to build the prose-writing instructions.

Format: one section per scene, in the order they appear in the chapter.

---

## Scene 1

### Identity
- **Scene label**: <e.g. "Opening — discovery in the library">
- **POV**: <character — usually inherited from chapter POV but can shift>
- **Location**: <specific place>
- **Time**: <when in the in-world day; how long after previous scene>
- **Approximate length**: <% of chapter, or word/character count>

### Cast
- **On-screen characters**: <list>
- **Mentioned but off-screen**: <list>

### Start state
What is the situation as the scene opens? One paragraph.
- Where are the characters physically?
- What just happened?
- What does each on-screen character WANT in this moment?
- What does the POV character know / not know?

### End state
What must be true when the scene ends? One paragraph.
- What has changed in the situation?
- What has changed in the POV character's understanding?
- What new fact / feeling does the reader walk away with?

### Required beats
Bullet list of beats that MUST happen in this scene:
- <beat — e.g. "Character A names the artifact for the first time">
- <beat — e.g. "Character B's hesitation is visible to the reader but not to character A">
- <beat>

### Forbidden items for this scene
Things that must NOT happen in THIS scene, even if they're fine in other scenes:
- <forbidden — e.g. "POV character does not yet realize what they're looking at">
- <forbidden — e.g. "No mention of [later plot element]">
- <forbidden — e.g. "Character C does not enter the room until next scene">

### Sensory anchor
One sense detail to ground the scene. (Helps prose stay specific instead of generic.)
- <e.g. "The library smells faintly of mildew under the lamp oil">

### Tone / pacing
- **Tempo**: <slow / measured / brisk / urgent>
- **Emotional register**: <one sentence>

### Connection to next scene
- **How this scene hands off to scene 2**: <one sentence>

---

## Scene 2

(Repeat the block above for each scene in the chapter.)

---

## Scene 3

...

---

## Notes for the Brief Agent

Anything the next stage needs to know about the chapter as a whole, that didn't fit into individual scenes:

- <note>
- <note>

---

## How Agents Use This File

- **Brief agent** reads all scene cards for the chapter, plus the plot file, plus relevant canon, and produces the final writing brief.
- **Prose agent** does NOT read this file directly (too much for one prompt). It reads the brief instead.
- **Plot review lens** checks the drafted chapter to verify each scene's "Required beats" landed and no "Forbidden items" appeared.

The scene card stage is where most structural problems get caught early — before any prose is generated. If a scene's start state, required beats, and end state don't add up, fix it here, not in the prose.

The master index and final-arbiter file for canonical facts about the story.

If something is contested across other canon files, the value in **this** file wins.
Most canonical facts should live in their specialized files (`character_bible.md`, `world_bible.md`, etc.). This file is for cross-cutting decisions, story-level facts, and the authoritative pointer to where everything else lives.

---

## Canonical Policy

- **Canon-promoted decisions** are locked. Agents cannot override them. To change canon, a human author must edit the source file.
- **Provisional decisions** are decisions made during drafting that may still change. Use `Provisional (YYYY-MM-DD)` markers in the source files.
- **Source-of-truth precedence (high → low)**:
  1. This file (`canon.md`)
  2. Specialized canon files (`character_bible.md`, `world_bible.md`, `glossary.md`, `timeline.md`)
  3. Style engine (`style_guide.md`, `forbidden_patterns.md`)
  4. Per-arc design files
  5. Per-chapter scene cards and briefs
  6. The drafts themselves (lowest authority — drafts are output, not source)

---

## Story-Level Canon

The handful of facts that define what makes this story THIS story. If you change any of these, you're writing a different story.

- **Genre / hybrid**: <e.g. "reincarnation fantasy with misperception comedy">
- **Core premise (one sentence)**: <the elevator pitch>
- **Protagonist's defining wound / drive**: <one sentence>
- **The promise to the reader**: <what you guarantee the story will deliver>
- **The thing you won't do**: <one or two anti-promises — what this story will NEVER become>

---

## Cross-File Indexing

Pointers to where specific canonical info lives:

| Topic | Lives in |
|---|---|
| Character names, roles, calling rules | `character_bible.md` |
| Detailed character voice and speech | `../03_project_design/characters/<NAME>.md` (if exists) |
| Locations, magic system, institutions | `world_bible.md` |
| Terminology and proper nouns | `glossary.md` |
| In-world dates and event sequence | `timeline.md` |
| Prose style rules | `../92_style_engine/style_guide.md` |
| Banned constructions and AI-tells | `../92_style_engine/forbidden_patterns.md` |

---

## Canon Change Log

Every promotion from Provisional → Canon, every demotion, every contested-then-resolved decision goes here:

| Date | Change | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| YYYY-MM-DD | <e.g. "Character X's calling pattern in private with Y: promoted to Canon"> | <reason> |
| YYYY-MM-DD | <change> | <reason> |

This log is for human review during arc-end canon passes. It is NOT loaded into agent context (would bloat too fast).

---

## Hard Rules (story-specific things agents must never do)

This section is where you encode the project's non-negotiables. Things that can't be expressed cleanly in `forbidden_patterns.md` (because they're not patterns, they're story facts).

Examples:

- "Character X never reveals their true name in dialogue."
- "The enemy faction's existence is not narrated directly in the protagonist's POV before chapter 60."
- "Magic system rule: no character can use [specific ability] without paying [specific cost]. Any draft that does is wrong."
- "[Character Y] is dead from chapter 15 onward and cannot appear except in flashback or as a corpse."

---

## How Agents Use This File

- **All agents** read `canon.md` first when given a task. It tells them which other files to consult and which non-negotiables apply.
- **Canon review lens** uses the Hard Rules section as a checklist against the draft.
- **Brief agent** uses the Story-Level Canon to keep every chapter aligned with the story's defining promises.

# Timeline

The canonical sequence of events in the story, plus the time each chapter covers and when characters reach which milestones.

Why this file exists: continuity errors love long projects. If chapter 12 says the journey takes 3 days and chapter 28 says it took 5, you need a single source of truth that catches the contradiction.

---

## Story Timeline (in-world dates)

| Date / Year | Event | Chapter |
|---|---|---:|
| Year 0 (story start) | <protagonist's age, world state> | ch1 |
| Year 0, Month 3 | <event> | ch5 |
| Year 1 | <event> | ch20 |

Use relative dates ("Year 0, Day 47") rather than real-world dates unless your story explicitly uses them. Relative dates are easier to keep consistent.

---

## Per-Chapter Time Coverage

| Chapter | Starts | Ends | Duration | POV |
|---|---|---|---:|---|
| ch1 | Year 0, Day 1, morning | Year 0, Day 1, evening | 1 day | <character> |
| ch2 | Year 0, Day 2, morning | Year 0, Day 5, night | 4 days | <character> |
| ch3 | Year 0, Day 6 | Year 0, Day 6 | 1 day | <character> |

This table is what the canon review lens uses to catch "chapter 12 happens AFTER chapter 14 but references events from chapter 13" errors.

---

## Character Ages / Milestones

| Character | Age at ch1 | Age at ch20 | Age at ch50 | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| <CHAR> | 10 | 12 | 15 | Birthday is in Month 4 |
| <CHAR> | 25 | 27 | 30 | |

If your story spans multiple in-world years, this is the table that prevents the "wait, isn't she still 10?" error in later chapters.

---

## Major Events (cross-chapter)

For events that have ripples across many chapters (a war, a death, a reveal), track them as anchored points:

| Event | Happens in | Referenced in | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| <EVENT> | ch15 | ch16, ch18, ch24, ch31 | Active reference |
| <EVENT> | ch7 | ch9, ch12 | Resolved by ch20 |

---

## Foreshadowing Ledger

If you do plant-and-payoff structure (especially important for mysteries and long-running series), track every planted seed here:

| Seed | Planted in | Payoff target | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| <SEED — one line> | ch3 | ch28 | Planted |
| <SEED> | ch7 | ch20 | Paid off in ch20 |
| <SEED> | ch12 | ch45 | Planted, needs reinforcement at ch30 |

The plot review lens checks this ledger and flags:
- Seeds that have been visible too long without movement (probably forgotten)
- Payoff chapters whose brief doesn't reference their planted seeds (will read as unmotivated)

For long series with deep foreshadowing, this is the most important table in the timeline file.

---

## How Agents Use This File

- **Brief agent** for chapter N reads the per-chapter time coverage of chapter N-1, ensuring the new chapter starts at a valid point in story-time.
- **Canon review lens** loads this whole file and catches date/age/duration contradictions.
- **Plot review lens** uses the foreshadowing ledger to verify setup and payoff land correctly.

When a chapter is finalized, update this file: add its time coverage, age any characters whose birthdays passed, mark any seeds as paid off.

# World Bible

The physical, social, and metaphysical laws of the story world.
If something is true about how the world works — and any character in any chapter could be affected by it — it lives here.

---

## Setting Overview

- **Genre**: <e.g. fantasy / sci-fi / mystery / contemporary>
- **Time period / equivalent**: <e.g. "early industrial revolution analog", "Heian-era Japan analog">
- **Geographic scope**: <e.g. "single kingdom", "multi-continent">
- **Tech / magic level**: <one paragraph summary>

---

## Geography

| Place | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| <PLACE NAME> | capital / town / region / continent | <role in story> |
| <PLACE NAME> | <type> | <notes> |

Travel times between major locations (relevant if the timeline.md references them):

| From → To | Method | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| <A> → <B> | <horse / train / portal> | <X days> |

---

## Political / Social Structure

- **Government type**: <e.g. constitutional monarchy, federation, tribal council>
- **Class structure**: <e.g. nobility / commoner / slave; or none>
- **Currency**: <name and rough purchasing power>
- **Languages**: <number, who speaks what>

---

## Magic / Tech System (if applicable)

Define the rules. The clearer the rules, the harder it is for AI to violate them by accident.

- **Source of power**: <where magic/tech comes from>
- **Cost**: <what does using it cost the user>
- **Limits**: <hard limits — what's impossible>
- **Common applications**: <typical everyday uses>
- **Rare / forbidden applications**: <what's possible but restricted>

---

## Institutions

For any organization that has its own rules, hierarchy, or culture (academies, guilds, churches, courts), give it a dedicated subsection:

### <INSTITUTION NAME>

- **Purpose**: <what it does>
- **Hierarchy**: <ranks, leadership>
- **Membership / access**: <who's in it, who's not>
- **Internal rules / culture**: <relevant for character behavior>

---

## Calendar / Time

- **Year length**: <e.g. 360 days, 4 seasons>
- **Week / month structure**: <if it matters>
- **Notable annual events**: <festivals, ceremonies, anniversaries the plot might use>

---

## Material Culture (only what matters for prose)

Don't write a complete anthropology. Document only what would surface in a scene:

- **Clothing**: <enough that the prose agent doesn't invent silk dresses in a Bronze Age setting>
- **Food**: <staples, status foods, taboos>
- **Transport**: <relevant to pacing>
- **Architecture**: <enough to set a scene>

---

## How Agents Use This File

- **Brief agent** extracts the world details relevant to a chapter's setting (if the chapter is set in <PLACE X>, pull the geography + institution details for <PLACE X>).
- **Canon review lens** loads this whole file and checks the draft for contradictions: travel time errors, magic-rule violations, institution misuse, anachronisms.
- **Plot review lens** uses the calendar to verify timeline consistency across chapters.

If a rule established here is broken by a chapter, the canon lens should flag it before the chapter is finalized.

# Glossary

Every proper noun, in-world term, or specialized vocabulary item in the story, with its canonical definition.

Why this file exists: AI models will happily invent synonyms, alternate spellings, or "creative" rewordings of your terminology if you don't lock it down. The glossary is the lock.

---

## Format

| Term | Definition | First Appearance | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| <TERM> | <one-sentence canonical definition> | ch1 | <usage notes, e.g. "always capitalized; never abbreviated"> |
| <TERM> | <definition> | ch5 | <notes> |

---

## Suggested Categories

For long projects, group terms by category. Examples:

### Places
| Term | Definition | First | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|

### Titles / Ranks
| Term | Definition | First | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|

### Magic / Tech Terms
| Term | Definition | First | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|

### Cultural / Religious Terms
| Term | Definition | First | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|

### In-World Slang / Idioms
| Term | Definition | First | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|

### Faction-Specific Vocabulary
Different factions may have different words for the same thing. Document the mapping:

| Concept | Faction A calls it | Faction B calls it | Reader knows it as |
|---|---|---|---|
| <CONCEPT> | <TERM> | <TERM> | <TERM> |

This is critical for multi-faction stories — agents writing from Faction A's POV must use Faction A's vocabulary, not the reader-default term.

---

## Character-Specific Vocabulary

Some characters have signature phrases or unique vocabulary tied to their voice. Document them here (or cross-reference to `character_voice_samples.md`):

| Character | Signature term / phrase | Meaning / use |
|---|---|---|
| <CHAR> | <PHRASE> | <when they say it, what it conveys> |

---

## How Agents Use This File

- **Brief agent** scans the chapter outline, identifies which glossary terms will appear, and includes their definitions in the prose prompt.
- **Style review lens** flags any in-world term that doesn't appear in this glossary (could be a typo, could be an invented term that needs to be added or removed).
- **Canon review lens** flags any glossary term used with the wrong meaning.

When a term is upgraded from invented-in-draft to canon, add it here. The glossary should grow with the story.
